section_summary: This section comprises press clippings, consular despatches, interdepartmental correspondence, and cross-reference records from 1935 (along with a 1947 State Department charge slip) concerning second-generation Japanese Americans (Nisei) residing, studying, or working in Japan, as well as broader U.S.-Japan educational and cultural exchanges. Key items document the cultural and economic adaptation of Nisei in Tokyo, including female performers introducing American jazz dance, a group of young Californians studying chick sexing in Nagoya to fill U.S. agricultural labor shortages, and survey data on Nisei living conditions and national loyalty. The records reflect ongoing administrative coordination between the Department of State, the Department of Labor, and the War Department regarding Japanese American immigration, technical training, and educational exchange initiatives.

subfiles.about: The concluding portion of an article discussing the economic difficulties, citizenship, national loyalty, and social status of Japanese Americans in both the United States and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The concluding portion of this article analyzes the historical transition of Japanese immigrants in America and the emerging problems confronting their American-born children. It observes that severe economic discrimination and professional exclusion in the United States have driven hundreds of Nisei to Japan, where some Japanese organizations erroneously treat them as Japanese rather than Americans. Emphasizing that Nisei remain loyal American citizens, the author urges Japanese educators and leaders to respect their American identity and calls upon American society to remove racial barriers and embrace their contributions.
subfiles.title: Article on the Role and Status of Second-Generation Japanese Americans

subfiles.about: A feature newspaper article profiling four American-born Japanese female performers introducing American jazz, tap, torch singing, and Hawaiian hula to Tokyo audiences.
subfiles.summary: Published as Enclosure No. 3(b) in The Japan Times & Mail, this illustrated article profiles four young Nisei women working in Tokyo's entertainment sector: Fumiko Kawabata, Helen Yukiko Honda, Betty Inada, and Helen Sumida. Each performer recounts her background on the American stage, her current recording and film engagements in Japan, and the challenge of educating local audiences to appreciate Western dance and musical styles. The entertainers reflect on their experiences of cultural adjustment, noting that while Japanese audiences are polite, they find it challenging to navigate cultural expectations and perform songs translated into Japanese.
subfiles.title: They Provide Torch Songs, High Kicks Or The Hula: Second Generation Girls Introducing American Dance

subfiles.about: An internal Department of State charge slip documenting the checkout of decimal file 894.42711.
subfiles.summary: This internal Department of State charge slip records the removal of file 894.42711 from central files. It is dated July 23, 1947, and notes the requesting or handling individual as R. E. Barber.
subfiles.title: Department of State Charge Slip for File 894.42711

subfiles.about: A consular despatch reporting the arrival in Nagoya of four Japanese American youths from California to study chick sexing at a local specialized training school.
subfiles.from: Charles H. Stephan, American Vice Consul, Nagoya, Japan
subfiles.summary: American Vice Consul Charles H. Stephan reports the informal registration of four American-born Japanese youths from California (Kiyoto Saiki, Clyde Koki Goto, Shinichi Ishikura, and one companion) who traveled to Nagoya for three months of intensive training at the Nagoya Sexers' Association Training School. The students intend to gain practical experience on poultry farms before returning to the United States in January 1936 to satisfy a large domestic demand for sexing specialists. The despatch quotes the Osaka Mainichi, noting that because expert chick sexers from Japan are classified as laborers and barred from U.S. entry under immigration laws, second-generation Japanese American citizens were recruited to acquire and preserve the technique.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 23 from Nagoya: American-Born Japanese Study Chick Sexing

subfiles.about: A transmittal note from the Secretary of State forwarding a copy of Nagoya Despatch No. 23 concerning chick sexing to the Secretary of Labor.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State transmits to the Secretary of Labor, for departmental information, an enclosed copy of Despatch No. 23 dated September 9, 1935, from the American Vice Consul at Nagoya entitled 'American-born Japanese Study Chick Sexing.' The communication is indexed in State Department records under file number 894.42711/3.
subfiles.title: Transmittal of Nagoya Despatch No. 23 to the Secretary of Labor

subfiles.about: A letter from the Immigration and Naturalization Service acknowledging receipt of Nagoya Despatch No. 23 on chick sexing.
subfiles.from: Henry B. Hazard, Acting Deputy Commissioner, Immigration and Naturalization Service, Department of Labor
subfiles.summary: Acting Deputy Commissioner Henry B. Hazard acknowledges receipt of the Department of State's communication of October 23, 1935, which enclosed a copy of Nagoya Despatch No. 23 on chick sexing training among American-born Japanese youths. The response references State Department file number 894.42711/3 and Labor Department file 55853/185-z. Page 251 contains an unexecuted carbon copy of the letter filed as 894.42711/4.
subfiles.title: Letter from Immigration and Naturalization Service Acknowledging Receipt of Nagoya Despatch No. 23
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State, Washington, D. C.

subfiles.about: A War Department routing slip transmitting a Japan Advertiser newspaper clipping summarizing a survey of second-generation Japanese residing in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The War Department Military Intelligence Division routed a newspaper clipping to the State Department Division of Far Eastern Affairs for informational filing under 894.42711/5. The attached Japan Advertiser article, titled 'Nippon Is Verdict,' reports on a survey of approximately one thousand Nisei in the Tokyo area regarding their adjustment to Japanese life. While most respondents appreciated living free from racial prejudice, many noted difficulties with the language, social rigidities, gender inequality, and lower standards of living; notably, nearly 99 percent indicated their intent to return to the United States or Hawaii.
subfiles.title: War Department Routing Slip and Clipping: 'Nippon Is Verdict'
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet recording correspondence from the Institute of Pacific Relations regarding Japanese graduate exchange students in the United States.
subfiles.from: Bruno Lasker, American Council, Institute of Pacific Relations
subfiles.summary: This Document File Note cross-references a letter dated August 9, 1935, from Bruno Lasker of the American Council, Institute of Pacific Relations, filed under 811.42794/66 and cross-indexed under 894.42711/6. The communication notes concern among Japanese educators regarding a decline in Japanese graduate students attending American institutions and highlights an exchange arrangement plan brought to the United States by Dr. Kenzo Takayanagi.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Japanese Exchange Students in the United States
